Run name is `<run>`; the phase you are running is `<phase>`.

1. **Start the phase — briefed.** drovr composes the brief (frame, scope, completion
   contract) and injects it; your `--context` is the part it cannot know, which across a
   handoff boundary is the PRIOR phase's handoff:
   ```
   drovr collect <run> <prev> > /tmp/<prev>-handoff.md   # prints <prev>-HANDOFF.md
   drovr phase start <run> <phase> --context-file /tmp/<prev>-handoff.md
   ```
   For the first phase there is no prior handoff — omit `--context` and the run's task
   carries it. Read exactly what the agent will be told with
   `drovr phase brief <run> <phase>`; do not retype or paraphrase it.

2. **Check it landed.** `phase start` prints `briefed phase '<phase>'` on success. If it
   exits 2 the pane is up but UNBRIEFED — re-deliver once the agent is at its composer:
   ```
   drovr phase brief <run> <phase> --context-file /tmp/<prev>-handoff.md \
     | drovr phase send <run> <phase> -
   ```
   `phase send` also stays available for free-form mid-flight nudges; a message is not a
   brief, and you never author the frame.

   The composed brief carries the **completion contract**, whose final two
   actions are, in order:
   1. **Author the handoff.** Write `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/<phase>-HANDOFF.md` — the
      fixed 7-section document (see `HANDOFF-template.md`), compressed from your own context,
      **git pointers mandatory**. This is *your* job as the finishing agent; nothing compresses
      it for you.
   2. **Signal done:** run `drovr phase done <run> <phase>`. It **refuses with an error until
      the handoff above exists, is non-empty, and has no section left at the scaffold's
      `TODO`** — the handoff and the done-marker are one atomic completion step, and a form
      still holding its placeholders carries nothing for the next phase to inherit. The
      error names the unfilled sections.

   Also tell the agent that any reviewers it dispatches must run in the **foreground**
   (never `run_in_background`, never yield waiting on them), so step 3 can detect completion.

3. **Wait for done — background the wait, then end your turn.**
   ```
   drovr phase wait <run> <phase> --timeout-ms 86400000     # Bash run_in_background: true
   ```
   Then **stop and end the turn immediately**: no other command, no edits, no scheduled
   wakeup. The harness wakes you with the exit code when the process exits — that notification
   *is* your synchronization signal. `drovr phase wait` is still the sync primitive; the only
   change is that the harness, not the Bash call, holds the block.

   **Why not foreground?** A foreground Bash call is hard-capped at **600 000 ms (10 min)** —
   you cannot ask for more. Real phases routinely run longer, so a foreground wait does not
   block until the phase finishes: it dies at the cap and reports exit `2` on a phase that is
   still running healthily. You then re-run it, burning a turn and a fresh context read every
   10 minutes. Backgrounding removes the cap — one wait, one wake-up, when the phase is
   actually done. It is also the only way a `--timeout-ms` above 600 000 is reachable at all.

   **The rule the old "always foreground" advice was protecting still holds**, and it is the
   part that matters: *never do your own work while a phase agent is writing.* That is drovr's
   single-writer rule, not a property of foreground-ness. Backgrounding is only dangerous if
   you keep working — so background the wait and go idle.

   This POLLS the filesystem for the marker the agent drops via `drovr phase done` (step 2's
   final action). Completion is that marker, never herdr's `idle` status — `idle` also fires
   while the agent is parked awaiting a reviewer or explorer of its own. **Note the default
   `--timeout-ms` is 30 000 (30 s), which is far too short for a real phase; always pass an
   explicit value.** Pass a long one — 86 400 000 (24 h) above: exit `2` only ever means
   "re-arm", and every re-arm is a turn spent learning nothing. A blocked agent ends the wait
   with exit `4` long before any timeout; what a long timeout gives up is noticing an agent that
   sits idle without finishing, so look at `drovr status <run>` if a phase is taking far longer
   than its work should.

   Handle the exit code the wake-up hands you:

   | Exit | Meaning | What to do |
   |---|---|---|
   | `0` | done — the handoff exists | Go to step 4. |
   | `4` | **blocked** — the agent hit a safety/permission prompt; the diagnostic names the class | Answer the prompt (`herdr agent send-keys <pane> …`), then **re-arm**. Do not treat this as failure. |
   | `2` | timed out; the phase may still be running healthily | **Re-arm**, or investigate if it has now timed out twice. |
   | `5` | **superseded** — a newer `phase start` re-entered the phase while this wait ran, so it was watching a pass that no longer exists | Nothing is wrong with the phase. **Re-arm** to follow the live pass. Never triage this as a stuck agent. |
   | `1` | I/O error | STOP — see *Stop conditions*. |

   ⚠️ **Do not pipe this command.** A shell pipeline's exit status is its **last** command's,
   so `drovr phase wait … | tail -5` reports `tail`'s 0 and every row above reads as `0` —
   done. Trimming output with `| tail`/`| head`/`| grep` is a natural habit and it voids this
   table silently. Capture the status instead:
   ```
   drovr phase wait <run> <phase> --timeout-ms 86400000; rc=$?; echo "EXIT=$rc"; exit $rc
   ```
   The same trap applies to every drovr command with an exit-code contract — `review wait`
   and `code-review run` most of all, where a swallowed status has already produced both a
   false approval and a false clean review.

   **Re-arm** = run the exact same backgrounded `drovr phase wait` again and end the turn again.
   The wait is stateless and resumable: it polls an on-disk marker, so nothing is lost by
   re-issuing it and a phase that finished during the gap is detected immediately.

   **`phase wait` only sees the phase you named.** It is the right tool while you are driving one
   phase and have nothing else in flight. When several agents are running — a panel, or two phases
   across two runs — background `drovr watch [<run>]` instead (or as well): it exits `4` the moment
   ANY of them stops on a prompt only a human can answer, and `0` when every agent has exited.
   Answer the prompt, then re-arm exactly as above. A `drovr ask` never ends it — a question is
   the human's to answer on the run's page, not yours — it only keeps the watch from exiting `0`.

4. **Collect + hand forward.**
   ```
   drovr collect <run> <phase>
   ```
   Prints the handoff (the file the agent authored). It becomes the next phase's
   `--context-file` in step 1 — drovr puts it in the brief it composes.

## Quick reference

| Step | Command | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **start (briefed)** | `drovr phase start <run> <phase> --context-file <prev handoff>` | composes the brief AND injects it; prints `briefed phase …`. Exit 2 = pane up but unbriefed |
| inspect | `drovr phase brief <run> <phase> [--context …]` | prints exactly what the agent is told, spawning nothing |
| re-brief | `drovr phase brief … \| drovr phase send <run> <phase> -` | for a phase already running; `phase send "<text>"` is for free-form nudges only |
| wait | `drovr phase wait <run> <phase> --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded, then end the turn**; polls for the `done` marker (not herdr idle). `0`=done → step 4 · `4`=blocked on a prompt → answer it, re-arm · `2`=timeout → re-arm · `5`=superseded by a newer pass → re-arm, not a stuck agent · `1`=io-error → stop. Default timeout is only 30 s — always override. Foreground Bash caps at 600 000 ms, so a foreground wait times out on healthy long phases |
| watch | `drovr watch [<run>] --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded**; exits when ANY agent (of the run, or of every run drovr can read) stops on a prompt drovr will not answer. `4`=needs a human, the report names the phase and quotes the prompt · `0`=nothing left to watch (every agent gone, every run's phases finished, AND no unanswered `drovr ask`) — an unanswered ask never ends the watch and is never reported, it only holds it open · `2`=timeout → re-arm · `1`=error, including any run whose state could not be read. Routine permission dialogs do not wake it — a running `phase wait` answers those. Safe to background BEFORE `phase start`: a run with phases outstanding keeps it watching |
| ask | `drovr ask <run> --question <text\|@file> [--context <text> \| --context-file <path> \| --context-html <path>] [--option <value>=<label>]... [--recommend <value>]` | run by the AGENT, never the driver: posts one question for the human and **returns immediately** — it never blocks and never waits. Prints three lines — the ask id, the reviewer's page URL (starting the review server if it is not already up; only a server that could not be started gets a note instead, and the question is on disk either way), and the `ask wait` command to background. `0`=posted · `5`=run cancelled (terminal — stop work, do not re-ask) · `1`=error. `--context`/`--context-file`/`--context-html` are mutually exclusive. `--context-html` takes a FILE of HTML — headings, tables, a `<style>` block — shown in a sandboxed frame beside the question, for a decision a paragraph of plain text renders badly. It is REFUSED, exit `1`, if the file does not parse, and the accepted subset is narrower than a browser's: every element closed, attributes quoted, `<` for a bare `<`, no script. `drovr ask preview <path>` runs the same check and writes the rendered document to a temp file you can open — use it before posting, not after. `@<path>` on `--question` reads the text from a file (`@@` escapes a leading `@`). The record is append-only in `<run_dir>/interview.jsonl`, so it survives the agent that posted it |
| ask wait | `drovr ask wait <run> --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded, then end the turn**; a file poller, so it works while the panel is down. `0`=every question it was armed on is answered — those asks, each with its latest answer, as JSON on stdout (**not** the whole log; earlier answered asks are not in it) · `2`=timeout → re-arm, **nothing is lost** (the question is still on disk and still on screen) · `5`=run cancelled · `1`=error, including a run dir that is not there. Nothing pending at start also exits `0`, and that case prints the whole folded interview rather than a bare `[]` |
| done | `drovr phase done <run> <phase>` | run by the AGENT as its final action; **refuses until `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` exists**; drops the marker `wait` polls |
| scaffold | `drovr handoff-scaffold <run> <phase>` | writes the empty 7 sections for the AGENT to fill; refuses to overwrite an authored one. Structure only — drovr does not guess which commits are yours. `phase done` refuses while any section is still `TODO` |
| collect | `drovr collect <run> <phase>` | reads `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` |

## The HANDOFF doc shape

The finishing agent authors a fixed 7-section document (objective · state · decisions+rationale ·
interfaces/contracts · open questions · next step · artifact pointers). See
`HANDOFF-template.md` in this directory for the contract and what each section is for.
**Artifact pointers are paths, not pasted content** — the next agent re-reads source on
demand (that is what keeps each phase's context small). Artifact pointers **must include git
references** — the branch and the commit range/SHAs carrying this phase's work — so the next
agent re-derives load-bearing decisions from `git log`/`git diff`, using history as a durable
cross-check against lossy compression rather than trusting the summary alone.

## Self-review before you author the handoff

If the phase produced an artifact (code, a spec, a plan), the phase agent should have
**reviewed its own work with read-only reviewers** and addressed their
Critical/Important findings *before* authoring the handoff and handing forward. Read-only
reviewers preserve the single-writer rule — they find, the phase agent fixes. Compressing an
unreviewed artifact just carries its defects into the next phase's briefing. (The
`drovr:pipeline` phase-prompts encode this per phase.)

## Stop conditions — a bad handoff cascades

If any of these happen, **STOP and surface diagnostics** rather than seeding the next phase
with a broken briefing:

- `drovr phase wait` exits `1` (failed) or keeps exiting `2` (never completes).
- `drovr phase done` keeps failing because the agent never authored the handoff, or
  `drovr collect` returns empty / missing the fixed sections.

Diagnose with `herdr agent read <pane>` (raw transcript), or `drovr attach <run>` to inspect
the pane live.
Seeding a fresh agent from a garbage handoff wastes the whole downstream chain — a broken
briefing is worse than a stopped run.

**Not a stop condition: `phase done` refusing with `$DROVR_PASS is not set`.** The marker must
carry the pass token the agent was launched under, so `drovr phase done` only works from inside
the phase's own pane. Run by hand from a plain shell it refuses — and prints the exact command
that would work, token included. The general form, for when you are composing it yourself:

```
DROVR_PASS=$(jq -r '.phases[]|select(.name=="<phase>").pass' <run_dir>/state.json) \
  drovr phase done <run> <phase>
```

`<run_dir>` is `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>`; a reviewer phase lives under
`.review_phases[]` instead. This is the escape hatch for a phase whose agent is gone but whose
work is finished — it bypasses the pane, not the contract: `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` must still
exist, with no `TODO` sections left.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Writing the brief yourself | drovr composes it. You supply `--context`; `phase brief` shows the result. A hand-written frame drifts from the contract and nothing detects it. |
| Ignoring exit 2 from `phase start` | The pane is up and UNBRIEFED. Re-deliver with `phase brief \| phase send -`; a `phase wait` on it never returns. |
| Expecting a separate compress step | There isn't one. The finishing agent authors the handoff itself, as its final action, before `phase done`. |
| `phase done` failing "handoff missing" | The agent must author `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` *before* running `phase done`; the marker won't drop without it. |
| `phase done` naming sections "still at the scaffold's TODO" | A scaffolded handoff was never filled in. Write those sections from your own context — nothing else will — then re-run. |
| Foregrounding `drovr phase wait` | Background it and end the turn. Foreground Bash is capped at 600 000 ms, so a long healthy phase reports a false exit `2`. |
| Backgrounding the wait and then working | Background the wait *and go idle*. The single-writer rule is what forbids working here, not foreground-ness. |
| Pasting file contents into the handoff | Use artifact pointers (paths + git refs); the successor re-reads. |
| Hardcoding `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` elsewhere | Read it via `drovr collect`; the finishing agent writes it directly (no CLI command authors it). |

| **start (briefed)** | `drovr phase start <run> <phase> --context-file <prev handoff>` | composes the brief AND injects it; prints `briefed phase …`. Exit 2 = pane up but unbriefed |
| inspect | `drovr phase brief <run> <phase> [--context …]` | prints exactly what the agent is told, spawning nothing |
| re-brief | `drovr phase brief … \| drovr phase send <run> <phase> -` | for a phase already running; `phase send "<text>"` is for free-form nudges only |
| wait | `drovr phase wait <run> <phase> --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded, then end the turn**; polls for the `done` marker (not herdr idle). `0`=done → step 4 · `4`=blocked on a prompt → answer it, re-arm · `2`=timeout → re-arm · `5`=superseded by a newer pass → re-arm, not a stuck agent · `1`=io-error → stop. Default timeout is only 30 s — always override. Foreground Bash caps at 600 000 ms, so a foreground wait times out on healthy long phases |
| watch | `drovr watch [<run>] --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded**; exits when ANY agent (of the run, or of every run drovr can read) stops on a prompt drovr will not answer. `4`=needs a human, the report names the phase and quotes the prompt · `0`=nothing left to watch (every agent gone, every run's phases finished, AND no unanswered `drovr ask`) — an unanswered ask never ends the watch and is never reported, it only holds it open · `2`=timeout → re-arm · `1`=error, including any run whose state could not be read. Routine permission dialogs do not wake it — a running `phase wait` answers those. Safe to background BEFORE `phase start`: a run with phases outstanding keeps it watching |
| ask | `drovr ask <run> --question <text\|@file> [--context <text> \| --context-file <path> \| --context-html <path>] [--option <value>=<label>]... [--recommend <value>]` | run by the AGENT, never the driver: posts one question for the human and **returns immediately** — it never blocks and never waits. Prints three lines — the ask id, the reviewer's page URL (starting the review server if it is not already up; only a server that could not be started gets a note instead, and the question is on disk either way), and the `ask wait` command to background. `0`=posted · `5`=run cancelled (terminal — stop work, do not re-ask) · `1`=error. `--context`/`--context-file`/`--context-html` are mutually exclusive. `--context-html` takes a FILE of HTML — headings, tables, a `<style>` block — shown in a sandboxed frame beside the question, for a decision a paragraph of plain text renders badly. It is REFUSED, exit `1`, if the file does not parse, and the accepted subset is narrower than a browser's: every element closed, attributes quoted, `<` for a bare `<`, no script. `drovr ask preview <path>` runs the same check and writes the rendered document to a temp file you can open — use it before posting, not after. `@<path>` on `--question` reads the text from a file (`@@` escapes a leading `@`). | ask wait | `drovr ask wait <run> --timeout-ms <ms>` | **run backgrounded, then end the turn**; a file poller, so it works while the panel is down. `0`=every question it was armed on is answered — those asks, each with its latest answer, as JSON on stdout (**not** the whole log; earlier answered asks are not in it) · `2`=timeout → re-arm, **nothing is lost** (the question is still on disk and still on screen) · `5`=run cancelled · `1`=error, including a run dir that is not there. The finishing agent authors a fixed 7-section document (objective · state · decisions+rationale ·
interfaces/contracts · open questions · next step · artifact pointers). See
`HANDOFF-template.md` in this directory for the contract and what each section is for.
**Artifact pointers are paths, not pasted content** — the next agent re-reads source on
demand (that is what keeps each phase's context small). Artifact pointers **must include git
references** — the branch and the commit range/SHAs carrying this phase's work — so the next
agent re-derives load-bearing decisions from `git log`/`git diff`, using history as a durable
cross-check against lossy compression rather than trusting the summary alone.

## Self-review before you author the handoff

If the phase produced an artifact (code, a spec, a plan), the phase agent should have
**reviewed its own work with read-only reviewers** and addressed their
Critical/Important findings *before* authoring the handoff and handing forward. Read-only
reviewers preserve the single-writer rule — they find, the phase agent fixes. Compressing an
unreviewed artifact just carries its defects into the next phase's briefing. (The
`drovr:pipeline` phase-prompts encode this per phase.)

## Stop conditions — a bad handoff cascades

If any of these happen, **STOP and surface diagnostics** rather than seeding the next phase
with a broken briefing:

- `drovr phase wait` exits `1` (failed) or keeps exiting `2` (never completes).
- `drovr phase done` keeps failing because the agent never authored the handoff, or
  `drovr collect` returns empty / missing the fixed sections.

the pane live.
Seeding a fresh agent from a garbage handoff wastes the whole downstream chain — a broken
briefing is worse than a stopped run.

carry the pass token the agent was launched under, so `drovr phase done` only works from inside
the phase's own pane. Run by hand from a plain shell it refuses — and prints the exact command
that would work, token included. The general form, for when you are composing it yourself:

```

  drovr phase done <run> <phase>
```

`.review_phases[]` instead. This is the escape hatch for a phase whose agent is gone but whose
work is finished — it bypasses the pane, not the contract: `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` must still
exist, with no `TODO` sections left.

|---|---|
| Writing the brief yourself | drovr composes it. You supply `--context`; `phase brief` shows the result. A hand-written frame drifts from the contract and nothing detects it. |
| Ignoring exit 2 from `phase start` | The pane is up and UNBRIEFED. Re-deliver with `phase brief \| phase send -`; a `phase wait` on it never returns. |
| Expecting a separate compress step | There isn't one. The finishing agent authors the handoff itself, as its final action, before `phase done`. |
| `phase done` failing "handoff missing" | The agent must author `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` *before* running `phase done`; the marker won't drop without it. |
| `phase done` naming sections "still at the scaffold's TODO" | A scaffolded handoff was never filled in. Write those sections from your own context — nothing else will — then re-run. |
| Foregrounding `drovr phase wait` | Background it and end the turn. Foreground Bash is capped at 600 000 ms, so a long healthy phase reports a false exit `2`. |
| Backgrounding the wait and then working | Background the wait *and go idle*. The single-writer rule is what forbids working here, not foreground-ness. |
| Pasting file contents into the handoff | Use artifact pointers (paths + git refs); the successor re-reads. |
| Hardcoding `<phase>-HANDOFF.md` elsewhere | Read it via `drovr collect`; the finishing agent writes it directly (no CLI command authors it). |

# HANDOFF: package the Orca GUI without the bwrap FHS sandbox

## 1. Objective

Replace `appimageTools.wrapType2` (a bubblewrap FHS sandbox) for the Orca GUI in
`orca.nix` with an unsandboxed package: the AppImage's extracted tree patched with
`autoPatchelfHook` and wrapped with `makeWrapper`, the way nixpkgs packages most
closed-source Electron apps (slack, discord, vscode). Done = the GUI runs on shiori
(Arch + Hyprland, no X server, non-NixOS) unsandboxed, is merged to master, and is
switched in with `hms`.

Why: the sandbox is the root of a run of bugs.
- Everything Orca spawns (its terminals, and the agents in them, this one included)
  lives inside it. `/etc/hostname` is missing, `date` prints UTC (`/etc/localtime`
  -> host file -> `/usr/share/zoneinfo`, which the sandbox's `/usr` replaces), and
  `/usr` is not Arch's.
- Fonts dangled the same way (every family fell to Montserrat Thin). The `fontsConf`
  workaround and `tests/sandbox-fonts.sh` exist only because of that.
- bwrap sits between every caller and the process and forwards no signals, and its
  `--die-with-parent` SIGKILLs the payload when its parent goes.

The original comment in `orca.nix` chose the sandbox because it "works on non-NixOS
hosts". That reason does not hold: a patchelf'd binary references store paths and
runs on Arch fine.

## 2. State

- master's `orca.nix`:
  - The GUI is `wrapType2` + nixGL. The bin is `orca-ide`, a wrapper that always adds
    `--ozone-platform=wayland`.
  - It has `extraBwrapArgs` for `FONTCONFIG_FILE=fontsConf`.
  - It has master's Mac-keybinding table and activation, which use `appimageContents`
    (extracted AppImage) for `app.asar`. Leave that work alone.
- **A parallel change is landing on master from another Orca session (the CLI work),
  touching the same file:**
  - `orca-ide` and `orca` become Orca's CLI, run on nixpkgs nodejs as
    `node ${appimageContents}/resources/app.asar.unpacked/out/cli/index.js`. No sandbox.
  - The GUI is renamed to `orca-ide-app`. The desktop Exec uses it, and so does
    `meta.mainProgram`.
  - The CLI env sets `ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE` to the GUI's `orca-ide-app`, so
    `orca-ide open` launches it.
  - Six Orca skills go into `~/.claude/skills`.

  Do not implement any of that here. Before merging, **rebase or merge onto
  origin/master and keep the GUI bin named `orca-ide-app`** (if the CLI change has
  landed by then).
- Nothing has been built for this task yet.

## 3. Decisions + rationale (already made, with the user)

- **Unsandbox the GUI with autoPatchelf; do not keep bwrap.**
- **Keep nixGL** (`config.lib.nixGL.wrap`). Without it, GBM/DRI look in the
  NixOS-only `/run/opengl-driver` and fall back to software rendering.
- **Keep the Wayland flag, conditional:** add `--ozone-platform=wayland` only when
  `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` is unset.
  - Hyprland has no X server, and Orca's startup gate picks X11 without it: a bare
    launch exits 1 with "needs a usable display server".
  - Node rejects the flag ("bad option", exit 9), and the CLI's `serve` probes
    `ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE` in node mode with a script as argv.
  - It also must not be injected into CLI dispatch. Master's always-on flag breaks
    `orca-ide open`: "Unknown flag --ozone-platform for command: open".
- **Plain exec wrapper only.** No shell that backgrounds the process, no signal
  forwarding. Unsandboxed, signals and exit codes reach Electron directly. That is
  the point of this change.
- Expect `fontsConf` / FONTCONFIG_FILE and `tests/sandbox-fonts.sh` to become
  unnecessary. With the host's `/usr` visible, fontconfig should see the host config.
  Verify before deleting either: Orca's default terminal font must still resolve to
  exactly "DejaVu Sans Mono" (`dejavu_fonts`).
- Electron's runtime needs: libsecret (safeStorage).

## 4. Interfaces / contracts

- The extracted AppImage (`pkgs.appimageTools.extract { inherit pname version src; }`)
  has:
  - `orca-ide`: the Electron binary.
  - `chrome-sandbox`, `chrome_crashpad_handler`, and the `.so`s next to them.
  - `resources/`, with more native ELF helpers that each need their libraries
    resolved: `orcad-template`, `relay`, `agent-browser-linux-x64`,
    `computer-use-linux`, `ripgrep`, `node-runtime`, `bin/orca-wayland-clipboard`,
    plus `app.asar.unpacked` native modules. Run `find -type f -exec file` to list
    them all.
- **chrome-sandbox:** Nix cannot make it setuid. Upstream's postinst only does that
  for hosts without unprivileged user namespaces; Arch has them. Confirm Chromium
  uses the namespace sandbox, and, if needed, decide between `--no-sandbox` and
  removing `chrome-sandbox` so it does not try the SUID path. Escalate to the user
  rather than silently disabling the Chromium sandbox.
- Desktop file: `orca-ide.desktop` with `Exec=AppRun %U` upstream. Rewrite Exec to
  the GUI bin. The scheme handler `x-scheme-handler/orca` must keep working. Install
  the hicolor icons 16..512 as now.
- Upstream's own `.deb` layout, for reference: `/usr/bin/orca-ide` -> CLI shim; GUI
  at `/opt/Orca/orca-ide`, not on PATH; desktop file `Exec=/opt/Orca/orca-ide %U`.

## 5. Open questions

- Does `autoPatchelfHook` resolve every helper in `resources/`? Some may dlopen libs
  (libGL/EGL, libsecret, libnotify) that need `runtimeDependencies` or
  `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.
- Does the bundled `node-runtime` / `orcad-template` need anything beyond patching?
  `orca-ide serve` uses orcad.
- Is `fontsConf` removable? Measure with fc-match from inside the running app's
  terminal.
- **CAUTION, you are running inside Orca.** Restarting or replacing the running Orca
  kills your own session. Test the new build as a second instance with its own
  profile, e.g. `--user-data-dir=$(mktemp -d)`, never by restarting the live app.
  Per the user's memory notes, eval-green plus a launched process is not "working":
  force a real render (open a window, a terminal tab) and check `coredumpctl` for
  crashes.

## 6. Next step

1. Create a branch in this worktree. Per memory, edits go in a worktree, never main
   on master.
2. Write a test first in `tests/`, committed to the repo per memory. It should fail
   now and pass after. Suggested claims:
   - the GUI bin is not a bwrap launcher;
   - `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 <gui> -p 1` prints 1;
   - `ldd` (or `patchelf --print-needed` plus resolution) of every ELF under the
     package has no "not found";
   - a launched second instance, with its own `--user-data-dir`, reports
     `TZ`/`date` and `/etc/hostname` as the host does, from a process it spawns.
3. Implement.
4. Review with drovr:code-review, to two consecutive clean rounds on an unchanged
   HEAD. No round cap; the user was explicit about that.
   - If the drovr panel can't run (it needs herdr; inside Orca it exits 1 on
     HERDR_SOCKET_PATH), use two read-only Explore reviewer agents per round
     instead: correctness+error-handling, and security+quality.
5. Merge to master, re-checking master first. Per memory, merge without asking.
6. Run `hms` (bare, never piped). Never `hms --local` unasked.

## 7. Artifact pointers

- Repo: `~/devel/dotfiles`. The file is `orca.nix`; it is imported from `home.nix`.
- master at the time of writing: `git log origin/master -- orca.nix`. Keybinding work
  is in `nix/orca-mac-keybindings*.js` and `tests/orca-mac-keybindings.sh`.
- Research branch `orca-cli-skills` at worktree
  `~/devel/dotfiles/.drovr/wt/orca-cli-skills`. It is being superseded, but its
  commit messages record what the sandbox broke, round by round:
  `git log origin/master..orca-cli-skills`. 9e53e6cc..d892f61a carry the findings;
  `tests/orca-cli-skills.sh` there has node-mode and signal probes worth reusing as
  checks that an unsandboxed build gets right for free.
- Upstream .deb (v1.4.238): https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/download/v1.4.238/orca-ide_1.4.238_amd64.deb
  Its `postinst` shows the CLI symlink and `chmod 4755 chrome-sandbox`.
- Release feed (version + sha512 source of truth):
  https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest/download/latest-linux.yml

5	  isDesktop = machine.gui or true;
6	
7	  # Orca (onorca.dev) — the agent IDE: parallel CLI agents, each in its own
8	  # worktree. Closed-source Electron app, not in nixpkgs (nixpkgs' `orca` is
9	  # the GNOME screen reader), so this packages the official Linux AppImage.
10	  # The electron-updater feed in each GitHub release, latest-linux.yml, is
11	  # the source of truth for version + sha512 when bumping: the yml's sha512
12	  # is the AppImage's, checked against
13	  # the download with `nix hash to-sri --type sha512 <sha512sum>`.
14	  # https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest/download/latest-linux.yml
15	  pname = "orca";
16	  version = "1.4.238";
17	  src = pkgs.fetchurl {
18	    url = "https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/download/v${version}/orca-linux.AppImage";
19	    hash = "REDACTED/sHSKlfJa4c1O2MCcdJhLrxCVm/NVKT+JtghzxoEsQ==";
20	  };
21	
22	  # Wrap the AppImage (not autoPatchelf of the .deb) so the Electron stack
23	  # runs in appimageTools' FHS env, which works on non-NixOS hosts. Electron
24	  # safeStorage wants libsecret at runtime.
25	  orca = pkgs.appimageTools.wrapType2 {
26	    inherit pname version src;
27	    extraPkgs = pkgs: [ pkgs.libsecret ];
28	    # The sandbox gets its own fontconfig, the way every other nix GUI app here
29	    # gets a nix-generated FONTCONFIG_FILE, instead of the distro's.
30	    # buildFHSEnv binds the host's /etc/fonts in, assuming NixOS; Arch's conf.d
31	    # links point into /usr/share/fontconfig, which the sandbox's /usr replaces,
32	    # so all of them dangled and every family fell to Montserrat Thin. See
33	    # fontsConf below. tests/sandbox-fonts.sh.
34	    extraBwrapArgs = [ "--setenv FONTCONFIG_FILE ${fontsConf}" ];
35	    # The AppImage ships bin/orca and an orca-ide.desktop; upstream's .deb
36	    # installs the CLI as `orca-ide`, and that is what the desktop Exec and
37	    # meta.mainProgram use below. appimageTools keeps the AppImage's own bin
38	    # name, so the wrapper is renamed by hand.
39	    #
40	    # --ozone-platform=wayland: Orca's startup gate picks X11 when neither
41	    # --ozone-platform nor ELECTRON_OZONE_PLATFORM_HINT says otherwise, and on
42	    # a Hyprland-only session there is no X server to stat — measured: the

{ config, lib, pkgs, machine, ... }:

let
  isDarwin = pkgs.stdenv.hostPlatform.isDarwin;
  isDesktop = machine.gui or true;

  # Orca (onorca.dev) — the agent IDE: parallel CLI agents, each in its own
  # worktree. Closed-source Electron app, not in nixpkgs (nixpkgs' `orca` is
  # the GNOME screen reader), so this packages the official Linux AppImage.
  # The electron-updater feed in each GitHub release, latest-linux.yml, is
  # the source of truth for version + sha512 when bumping: the yml's sha512
  # is the AppImage's, checked against
  # the download with `nix hash to-sri --type sha512 <sha512sum>`.
  # https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/latest/download/latest-linux.yml
  pname = "orca";
  version = "1.4.238";
  src = pkgs.fetchurl {
    url = "https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases/download/v${version}/orca-linux.AppImage";
    hash = "REDACTED/sHSKlfJa4c1O2MCcdJhLrxCVm/NVKT+JtghzxoEsQ==";
  };

  # Wrap the AppImage (not autoPatchelf of the .deb) so the Electron stack
  # runs in appimageTools' FHS env, which works on non-NixOS hosts. Electron
  # safeStorage wants libsecret at runtime.

    inherit pname version src;
    extraPkgs = pkgs: [ pkgs.libsecret ];
    # The sandbox gets its own fontconfig, the way every other nix GUI app here
    # gets a nix-generated FONTCONFIG_FILE, instead of the distro's.
    # buildFHSEnv binds the host's /etc/fonts in, assuming NixOS; Arch's conf.d
    # links point into /usr/share/fontconfig, which the sandbox's /usr replaces,
    # so all of them dangled and every family fell to Montserrat Thin. See
    # fontsConf below. tests/sandbox-fonts.sh.
    extraBwrapArgs = [ "--setenv FONTCONFIG_FILE ${fontsConf}" ];
    # The AppImage ships bin/orca and an orca-ide.desktop; upstream's .deb
    # installs the CLI as `orca-ide`, and that is what the desktop Exec and
    # meta.mainProgram use below. appimageTools keeps the AppImage's own bin
    # name, so the wrapper is renamed by hand.
    #
    # --ozone-platform=wayland: Orca's startup gate picks X11 when neither
    # --ozone-platform nor ELECTRON_OZONE_PLATFORM_HINT says otherwise, and on
    # a Hyprland-only session there is no X server to stat — measured: the
    # bare launch exits 1 with "needs a usable display server", and the
    # explicit wayland switch keeps it running (timeout kill at 20s, exit 124).
    # An env var would work from a shell but not a desktop-file launch, so it
    # is a flag on the command line.
    #
    # The flag lands in extraInstallCommands, not postFixup: wrapType2 is a
    # buildFHSEnv, whose buildCommand short-circuits genericBuild's phase
    # list, so postFixup never runs. The bin/orca symlink from buildCommand
    # is replaced with a wrapper that prepends the flag and passes "$@"
    # through. buildFHSEnv's builder has no makeWrapper on PATH, so its setup
    # hook is sourced by hand; and the wrapper must not target its own path
    # (renaming to orca-ide and wrapping orca-ide in place makes it exec
    # itself), so the bwrap launcher moves aside to .orca-ide-unwrapped.
    extraInstallCommands = ''
      source ${pkgs.makeWrapper}/nix-support/setup-hook
      mv $out/bin/orca $out/bin/.orca-ide-unwrapped
      makeShellWrapper $out/bin/.orca-ide-unwrapped $out/bin/orca-ide \
        --add-flags '--ozone-platform=wayland'
      install -Dm444 ${appimageContents}/orca-ide.desktop \
        $out/share/applications/orca-ide.desktop
      for size in 16 24 32 48 64 128 256 512; do
        install -Dm444 \
          ${appimageContents}/usr/share/icons/hicolor/''${size}x''${size}/apps/orca-ide.png \
          $out/share/icons/hicolor/''${size}x''${size}/apps/orca-ide.png
      done
      substituteInPlace $out/share/applications/orca-ide.desktop \
        --replace-fail 'Exec=AppRun' 'Exec=orca-ide'
    '';
    meta.mainProgram = "orca-ide";
  };
  # Hermetic: nixpkgs' own conf.d (store paths, the full standard alias set),
  # whose 50-user.conf pulls in ~/.config/fontconfig -- home-manager's font
  # dirs, i.e. the nix-profile fonts every other app here uses. Plus DejaVu:
  # Orca's Linux terminalFontFamily default is exactly "DejaVu Sans Mono" with
  # no fallback, and Chromium refuses fontconfig's alias to another mono font,
  # so without it the terminal lays a proportional fallback out on a mono grid.
  # Scoped to orca rather than the profile because only orca hardcodes it.
  fontsConf = pkgs.writeText "orca-fonts.conf" ''

## NO EMAILS

**Never write an email address into anything.** Not into files, commit messages,
docs, notes, handoffs or scratch files — mine, colleagues', or service accounts.
This repo is public, and an address is a durable identifier that spreads: it
leaks the work/personal boundary, it enumerates people, and once written it gets
copied onward.

Refer to an account by its **role** — "the personal Google account", "the work
account", "the project's GCS service agent" — or record the command that
recovers the identity at read time (`gcloud config get-value account`) rather
than pasting its output. Role-based wording is better documentation anyway: "must
be the personal account, not the work one" survives an address change; a pasted
address does not.

If an address seems genuinely load-bearing, ask first.

The exception is the git identity already configured in `home.nix`, which git
requires and which is on every commit regardless.

## Commit and Push Policy

This is a personal dotfiles repo on `master`. When asked to commit and push, do both without asking for confirmation. The global "ask before public communications" rule does not apply here.

## Applying config: use `hms`, not `home-manager switch`

`hms` (defined in `home.nix`, documented in `README.md`) pushes, waits for the
commit's CI run on `forge.ko.ag`, then switches — so the switch is a download of
the closure the in-cluster runner built, not a local compile. Expect it to block
for ten-odd minutes. `hms --local` builds here instead.

It refuses on a dirty tree and on a diverged checkout — **both refusals are
the feature.** CI can only build a pushed commit, so do not route around them
with a bare `home-manager switch` — commit and push, or pass `--local`
deliberately and say that you did.

A checkout on master that is strictly behind `origin/master` fast-forwards to
the fetched SHA and continues — no refusal, nothing to decide.

If a run goes red, `hms` prints the job's `error:` lines; read those rather than
re-running blind. Background on why CI is worth waiting for — and the 600s attic
transfer ceiling that made it unreliable for its first 61 runs — is in
`docs/ci-nix-home.md`.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for the claims orca.nix makes about the Orca CLI and its agent skills:
# that `orca-ide` and `orca` are the CLI and run from any shell, not only an
# Orca terminal; that the GUI is `orca-ide-app` and the CLI can launch it; and
# that the skills in ~/.claude/skills are the bytes this Orca build expects.
#
# Why this needs a test. Orca's own installer only reaches an Orca terminal: it
# puts a shim dir on PATH there (ORCA_CLI_BIN_DIR) and symlinks
# ~/.local/bin/orca-ide at a raw /nix/store path, a script that runs Electron
# against the host's libraries. The skills are stubs that tell the agent to
# run `orca-ide skills get <name>` outside an Orca terminal, so a skill without
# a working CLI under that name is a dead end. And the skills are pinned to a
# commit separately from the AppImage version; bumping one without the other
# silently installs guides for a different CLI. Orca ships the expected hashes
# in resources/skills/current-manifest.json, so that is what the files are
# held to.
#
# Usage:
#   tests/orca-cli-skills.sh    eval + build this host's config and test it

set -u
set -o pipefail

fails=0; n=0
pass() { n=$((n+1)); echo "ok   $1"; }
fail() { n=$((n+1)); echo "FAIL $1: $2"; fails=$((fails+1)); }
T=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$T"' EXIT

FLAKE=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)
# /etc/hostname is what CI writes to say which host it is; Orca's sandbox does
# not bind it in, so fall back to uname -n there.
HM="$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$(cat /etc/hostname 2>/dev/null || uname -n).config"
SKILLS="orca-cli orchestration computer-use orca-per-workspace-env orca-linear linear-tickets"

pkg_attr() { # pkg_attr <pname> <attr>
  nix eval --raw "$HM.home.packages" \
    --apply "ps: (builtins.head (builtins.filter (p: (p.pname or \"\") == \"$1\") ps)).$2"
}
drv=$(pkg_attr orca-cli drvPath) || { echo "no orca-cli in home.packages here" >&2; exit 1; }
want_version=$(pkg_attr orca-cli version) && [ -n "$want_version" ] \
  || { echo "orca-cli has no version" >&2; exit 1; }
CLI=$(nix-store --realise "$drv" | tail -1) || { echo "could not build orca-cli" >&2; exit 1; }
gui_drv=$(pkg_attr orca drvPath) || { echo "no orca in home.packages here" >&2; exit 1; }
GUI=$(nix-store --realise "$gui_drv" | tail -1) || { echo "could not build orca" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $CLI and $GUI"

# The skills' own rule: outside an Orca terminal, on Linux, the CLI is
# `orca-ide`; elsewhere it is `orca`. Both names must be the CLI, and the GUI
# must not also claim `orca-ide` -- in the profile it would shadow one of them.
for b in orca orca-ide; do
  if [ -x "$CLI/bin/$b" ]; then pass "orca-cli provides bin/$b"
  else fail "bin/$b" "missing from $CLI"; fi
done
if [ -x "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" ] && [ ! -e "$GUI/bin/orca-ide" ]; then
  pass "the GUI is orca-ide-app and leaves orca-ide to the CLI"
else fail "GUI bin names" "$(ls "$GUI/bin" | paste -sd' ')"; fi

# No sandbox between the caller and the CLI: a plain exec of node, so
# signals and exit codes are the CLI's own.
if grep -q 'exec .*/bin/node ' "$CLI/bin/orca-ide" && ! grep -q bwrap "$CLI/bin/orca-ide"; then
  pass "the CLI is a plain exec of node"
else fail "CLI launcher" "$CLI/bin/orca-ide is not a plain node exec"; fi

# `orca-ide open` spawns ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE, or else process.execPath --
# which under plain node is node itself. Exactly the profile's GUI: the
# unwrapped one has an orca-ide-app too, minus nixGL.
app=$(sed -nE 's|.*ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE:-([^}]*)\}.*|\1|p' "$CLI/bin/orca-ide")
if [ "$app" = "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" ]; then
  pass "orca open launches the profile's nixGL-wrapped GUI"
else fail "ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE" "'${app:-unset}', want $GUI/bin/orca-ide-app"; fi

# The GUI's --ozone-platform=wayland must stay out of node mode: the CLI's
# `serve` probes ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE with ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 and a
# script as argv, and Node rejects the flag ("bad option", exit 9).
out=$(ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 timeout 60 "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" -p '"node-ok"' 2>"$T/node-err")

#   tests/orca-cli-skills.sh    eval + build this host's config and test it

set -u
set -o pipefail

fails=0; n=0
pass() { n=$((n+1)); echo "ok   $1"; }
fail() { n=$((n+1)); echo "FAIL $1: $2"; fails=$((fails+1)); }
T=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$T"' EXIT

FLAKE=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)
# /etc/hostname is what CI writes to say which host it is; Orca's sandbox does
# not bind it in, so fall back to uname -n there.
HM="$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$(cat /etc/hostname 2>/dev/null || uname -n).config"
SKILLS="orca-cli orchestration computer-use orca-per-workspace-env orca-linear linear-tickets"

pkg_attr() { # pkg_attr <pname> <attr>
  nix eval --raw "$HM.home.packages" \
    --apply "ps: (builtins.head (builtins.filter (p: (p.pname or \"\") == \"$1\") ps)).$2"
}
drv=$(pkg_attr orca-cli drvPath) || { echo "no orca-cli in home.packages here" >&2; exit 1; }
want_version=$(pkg_attr orca-cli version) && [ -n "$want_version" ] \
  || { echo "orca-cli has no version" >&2; exit 1; }
CLI=$(nix-store --realise "$drv" | tail -1) || { echo "could not build orca-cli" >&2; exit 1; }
gui_drv=$(pkg_attr orca drvPath) || { echo "no orca in home.packages here" >&2; exit 1; }
GUI=$(nix-store --realise "$gui_drv" | tail -1) || { echo "could not build orca" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $CLI and $GUI"

# The skills' own rule: outside an Orca terminal, on Linux, the CLI is
# `orca-ide`; elsewhere it is `orca`. Both names must be the CLI, and the GUI
# must not also claim `orca-ide` -- in the profile it would shadow one of them.
for b in orca orca-ide; do
  if [ -x "$CLI/bin/$b" ]; then pass "orca-cli provides bin/$b"
  else fail "bin/$b" "missing from $CLI"; fi
done
if [ -x "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" ] && [ ! -e "$GUI/bin/orca-ide" ]; then
  pass "the GUI is orca-ide-app and leaves orca-ide to the CLI"
else fail "GUI bin names" "$(ls "$GUI/bin" | paste -sd' ')"; fi

# No sandbox between the caller and the CLI: a plain exec of node, so
# signals and exit codes are the CLI's own.
if grep -q 'exec .*/bin/node ' "$CLI/bin/orca-ide" && ! grep -q bwrap "$CLI/bin/orca-ide"; then
  pass "the CLI is a plain exec of node"
else fail "CLI launcher" "$CLI/bin/orca-ide is not a plain node exec"; fi

# `orca-ide open` spawns ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE, or else process.execPath --
# which under plain node is node itself. Exactly the profile's GUI: the
# unwrapped one has an orca-ide-app too, minus nixGL.
app=$(sed -nE 's|.*ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE:-([^}]*)\}.*|\1|p' "$CLI/bin/orca-ide")
if [ "$app" = "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" ]; then
  pass "orca open launches the profile's nixGL-wrapped GUI"
else fail "ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE" "'${app:-unset}', want $GUI/bin/orca-ide-app"; fi

# The GUI's --ozone-platform=wayland must stay out of node mode: the CLI's
# `serve` probes ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE with ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 and a
# script as argv, and Node rejects the flag ("bad option", exit 9).
out=$(ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 timeout 60 "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" -p '"node-ok"' 2>"$T/node-err")
if [ "$out" = node-ok ]; then
  pass "orca-ide-app runs in node mode (serve's runtime probe)"
else fail "orca-ide-app node mode" "${out:-$(tail -1 "$T/node-err")}"; fi

# `orca-ide open` spawns the GUI detached, then exits. Each GUI wrapper layer
# execs the next, so the GUI's bwrap is the CLI's own child; with
# --die-with-parent it would be SIGKILLed the moment `open` returns.
bash -c 'ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$1" -e "
  setTimeout(() => require(\"fs\").writeFileSync(process.argv[1], \"alive\"), 3000);
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 4000);" "$2" >/dev/null 2>&1 &' _ "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" "$T/alive"
for _ in $(seq 75); do [ -s "$T/alive" ] && break; sleep 0.2; done
if [ -s "$T/alive" ]; then pass "the GUI outlives the parent that spawned it (orca-ide open)"
else fail "GUI lifetime" "payload died with its spawning parent"; fi

# The manifest travels with the extracted AppImage, which the CLI's script
# references, so it is in the CLI's closure.
contents=$(nix-store -qR "$CLI" | while read -r p; do
  [ -f "$p/resources/skills/current-manifest.json" ] && echo "$p"; done | head -1)
[ -n "$contents" ] || { echo "no extracted AppImage in the closure of $CLI" >&2; exit 1; }
manifest="$contents/resources/skills/current-manifest.json"

# Outside an Orca terminal: none of its env, none of its shim dir on PATH.
# ${!ORCA_@}, not compgen: CI's bash is built without programmable completion.
clean_path=$(printf '%s' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | grep -v 'linux-orca-cli-shim' | paste -sd:)
outside() {
  local u=() v
  for v in ${!ORCA_@}; do u+=(-u "$v"); done
  env "${u[@]}" PATH="$clean_path" "$@"
}

got=$(outside "$CLI/bin/orca" --version 2>&1)
if printf '%s' "$got" | grep -qwF "$want_version"; then pass "orca --version reports $want_version outside Orca"
else fail "orca --version" "got '$got', want $want_version"; fi

# What every skill stub runs, under both names the stubs choose between.
for b in orca-ide orca; do
  got=$(outside "$CLI/bin/$b" skills get orca-cli 2>&1)
  if printf '%s' "$got" | grep -q '^# Orca CLI'; then pass "$b skills get orca-cli prints the guide outside Orca"
  else fail "$b skills get" "$(printf '%s' "$got" | head -3)"; fi
done

# A CLI failure is the CLI's exit status, not swallowed by a wrapper.
outside "$CLI/bin/orca-ide" no-such-command >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?
if [ "$rc" -eq 1 ]; then pass "an unknown command exits 1"
else fail "exit status" "unknown command exited $rc"; fi

# The rev is pinned by hand next to the version; the app knows its own.
rev=$(nix eval --raw "$HM.home.file" --apply 'f: f.".claude/skills/orca-cli".source' | sed -nE 's|.*-orca-skills-([0-9a-f]{40})/.*|\1|p')
if [ -n "$rev" ] && grep -aqF "sourceCommit:\`$rev\`" "$contents/resources/app.asar"; then
  pass "skills rev ${rev:0:8} is this build's sourceCommit"
else fail "skills rev" "'${rev:-unparsed}' is not the sourceCommit in app.asar"; fi

for s in $SKILLS; do
  src=$(nix eval --raw "$HM.home.file" --apply "f: toString f.\".claude/skills/$s\".source" 2>/dev/null) \
    || { fail "$s" "no home.file .claude/skills/$s"; continue; }
  # The source is a subpath of a fetch; realise the fetch's derivation itself.
  srcdrv=$(nix eval --raw "$HM.home.file" --apply \
    "f: builtins.head (builtins.attrNames (builtins.getContext f.\".claude/skills/$s\".source))" 2>/dev/null)
  nix-store --realise "$srcdrv" >/dev/null
  # Every file the manifest lists for the skill, as "<sha256>  <path>" lines.
  want=$(jq -r --arg n "$s" '.skills[] | select(.name == $n) | .files[] | "\(.exactSha256)  \(.path)"' "$manifest")
  [ -n "$want" ] || { fail "$s" "no entry in the manifest"; continue; }
  if out=$(cd "$src" 2>/dev/null && printf '%s\n' "$want" | sha256sum --quiet -c - 2>&1); then
    pass "$s matches this build's manifest ($(printf '%s\n' "$want" | wc -l) files)"
  else fail "$s" "${out:-$src is missing}"; fi
done

printf '\n%d/%d passed\n' "$((n-fails))" "$n"
[ "$fails" -eq 0 ]

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
orca: CLI on plain node as `orca-ide`/`orca`, six agent skills; GUI is `orca-ide-app`

Install Orca's CLI the way upstream's .deb lays it out: `orca-ide` on
PATH is the CLI, and the GUI is off that name (here `orca-ide-app`, used
by the desktop Exec). Orca's skills tell agents outside an Orca terminal
to run exactly `orca-ide`; master had the GUI there, with an always-on
--ozone-platform=wayland that broke the GUI binary's own CLI dispatch
("Unknown flag --ozone-platform for command: open").

The CLI is plain JavaScript, so it runs on nixpkgs' nodejs_24 (Electron
43 bundles node 24) as a plain exec -- no sandbox between the caller and
the CLI. ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE points `orca-ide open` at the nixGL-wrapped
GUI; NODE_OPTIONS is handed over as upstream's shim does.

GUI: the wayland flag only outside node mode (`serve` probes the GUI
with ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1, and Node rejects it); dieWithParent off,
since the GUI that `open` spawns is the CLI's direct child.

Six skills (orca-cli, orchestration, computer-use, orca-per-workspace-env,
orca-linear, linear-tickets) from stablyai/orca at the AppImage's own
sourceCommit; tests/orca-cli-skills.sh holds them to the hashes in the
build's current-manifest.json and the rev to the sourceCommit.

Supersedes the orca-cli-skills branch, which ran the CLI inside bwrap
and needed a hand-written signal forwarder to stop `serve` cleanly.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline -1; git diff --stat origin/master..HEAD

The GUI session is working. It's writing its test harness and using `systemd-run --user` to run checks outside Orca's sandbox.

**Status:** step 1 is built on a fresh branch, `orca-cli-node` (commit `63f565eb`). `tests/orca-cli-skills.sh` passes 18/18. The other Orca suites still pass: 5/5 fonts and 32/32 keybindings. `orca-ide status` and `orca-ide open` both work against the running app. Review round 1 is running. Merge and `hms` follow two clean rounds in a row, with no cap on rounds.

**What's on the branch:**
- **CLI:** `orca-ide` and `orca` run Orca's CLI on nixpkgs' Node 24 (Electron 43 bundles 24.22, nixpkgs has 24.21). The wrapper is a plain exec: no sandbox, no signal forwarding.
- **GUI:** renamed `orca-ide-app`. The Wayland flag is now added only outside node mode, which fixes the `Unknown flag --ozone-platform` error you hit. It no longer dies with its parent, so `orca-ide open` doesn't kill the window it starts.
- **Skills:** the same six as before, pinned and checked against the app's own hashes.
- **Size:** about 240 lines across the three files, including the test.

The old `orca-cli-skills` branch is now superseded. I'll delete its worktree once this lands.

  ## Review: origin/master..HEAD (63f565eb, "orca: CLI on plain node as `orca-ide`/`orca`, six agent skills; GUI is `orca-ide-app`")
  
  I read the full diff, the commit message, the six fetched SKILL.md files (`/nix/store/REDACTED/skills/*`), upstream's `resources/bin/orca-ide` shim, the CLI runtime sources (`out/cli/runtime/{launch,orca-app-executable,serve-app-launcher}.js`), `.forgejo/workflows/nix-eval.yml`, and the skills wiring in home.nix (lines 2296-2329). I wrote nothing.
  
  ### Critical
  None.
  
  ### Important
  
  **1. The GUI-lifetime case passes even if `dieWithParent = false` is reverted** (tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:80-88, guarding orca.nix:38)
  - The test starts the payload in the background from `bash -c '... &'`, and that shell exits immediately.
  - `--die-with-parent` uses `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`, which bwrap sets only once it is running. If the parent is already gone by then, the process has been reparented and the signal never fires.
  - The real `orca-ide open` keeps node alive while it waits on profile metadata, which is why the real bug showed up.
  - I checked this with bwrap directly, writing no files (stdout piped to `cat`):
    - `bash -c 'bwrap --die-with-parent ... sh -c "sleep 2; echo alive" &'` printed `alive`. That is the same shape as the test, and the payload survived even with die-with-parent on.
    - `bash -c 'bwrap --die-with-parent ... & sleep 0.5'` printed nothing: the payload was killed.
  - So the case cannot go red on the regression it claims to catch. The GUI wrapper chain (nixGL, then orca-ide-app, then the FHS launcher) only lengthens the gap.
  - Fix: keep the spawning parent alive past bwrap's startup, e.g. `... & sleep 2` inside the `bash -c`, and move the payload's write to about 5s. Then confirm the case goes red with `dieWithParent = true`.
  
  **2. The `orca` symlink goes against upstream and the skills it is meant to serve** (orca.nix:108 and :135; asserted at tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:50-53)
  - All six skills say: on Linux outside an Orca terminal use `orca-ide`, and "Never run bare `orca` there", because it is usually the GNOME screen reader.
  - Upstream's shim says its Linux name is `orca-ide` to "avoid[] Ubuntu GNOME Orca conflict". `serve-app-launcher.js` says "a bare `orca` there is often the screen reader".
  - Inside an Orca terminal, Orca's own shim directory supplies `orca`.
  - So no skill path in this Linux-only profile reaches `$out/bin/orca`. It can still collide with nixpkgs' `pkgs.orca` (screen reader, also pname `orca`, a buildEnv conflict if it is ever added) or shadow `/usr/bin/orca` depending on PATH order.
  - The comment "their name for it elsewhere" is accurate only for macOS/Windows and inside Orca terminals, none of which this binary covers. Consider dropping the link.
  
  **3. Risky third-party text installed globally into every Claude session** (orca.nix:255-258, list at :160-163)
  - All six stubs say: "If it fails with `runtime_access_denied`, your sandbox blocked the connection: re-run it with escalated permissions". That tells agents to ask for a sandbox escape, and they do it on Orca's say-so.
  - The stubs also tell agents to start the GUI themselves (`ORCA open --json`). With `dieWithParent = false`, that window outlives the agent.
  - `computer-use` lets agents drive any visible native window, including external Chrome/Safari with the user's live sessions.
  - These are pinned and hash-checked, and the permission system still gates escalation. But they now load in every `~/.claude` session, not only in Orca terminals. That is a deliberate exposure the commit message does not mention.
  - `orca-linear` and `linear-tickets` are byte-identical apart from the name. `linear-tickets` is labelled "Legacy bundled name ... kept so existing installs converge", which a fresh Nix install doesn't need. Both also overlap the repo's own `linear-flow` skill (home.nix:2297) on "working from a linked Linear issue", which makes triggering ambiguous. I suggest dropping `linear-tickets` and deciding deliberately about `orca-linear` vs `linear-flow`.
  
  ### nit
  - **tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:98: the comment is wrong.** "CI's bash is built without programmable completion" is false. `nixpkgs/29916453...#bash` (TOOLS_REV) builds `bash-interactive-5.3p9`, and there both `${!ORCA_@}` and `compgen -v ORCA_` work. `env "${u[@]}"` with an empty array under `set -u` also works there. The code is fine; only the stated reason is wrong.
  - **orca.nix:116-117 and tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:64-66: the fallback is described wrongly.** Both say that without `ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE` the CLI falls back to `process.execPath` (node). Under plain node, `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` is unset, so `open` throws `runtime_open_failed` (launch.js) and `serve` is refused outright by `canStartOrcaServer` (serve-app-launcher.js:16-19). The variable is what makes `serve` allowed at all, which the comment doesn't say.
  - **tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:33 duplicates orca.nix:160-163.** A skill added in orca.nix would go untested. Deriving the list from `home.file` attrNames matching `.claude/skills/` would avoid that.
  - **tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:83-88: the background payload is never tracked or killed.** It exits itself after 4s. But if node mode were ever not honoured, the test would leave a full GUI window running, and on early `exit 1` paths it may write into the already-deleted `$T`. Capturing the PID and killing it in the EXIT trap would be cleaner.
  - **tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:131:** `nix-store --realise "$srcdrv"` is unchecked. A failure only shows up later as "$src is missing", which is still a correct FAIL. It also realises the same drv six times.
  - **tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:123:** `nix eval` stderr is not silenced, so the `recurseIntoAttrs` evaluation warning adds noise to the output. Lines 126/129 already use `2>/dev/null`.
  
  ### Checks with no findings
  - **Secrets:** `outside()` passes only variable names (`${!ORCA_@}`) to `env -u`. Nothing echoes values, there is no `set -x`, and failure messages print only CLI output. `ORCA_AGENT_HOOK_TOKEN`'s value is never printed.
  - **Privacy:** no emails or private data in the diff.
  - **Temp dir:** `mktemp -d` plus an EXIT trap (line 27), the same pattern as sandbox-fonts.sh.
  - **CI tools:** the script uses only coreutils (mktemp, timeout, seq, paste, tr, sha256sum, uname), grep, sed, jq, nix and nix-store, all supplied by the `nix shell` in nix-eval.yml. No python3 or util-linux.
  - **CI GUI case:** the node-mode case runs the GUI under bwrap plus nixGL (mesa) in the privileged container. It needs no GPU or display, but I could not confirm a CI run.
  - **CLI on plain node:** the CLI's external requires are only `node:*`, `zod` and `@orca/process-host`. The one native module, sherpa-onnx in serve-speech-recognizer, is loaded by the app side. The bundled Electron reports node 24.22.0, so the "same major" claim holds.
  - **NODE_OPTIONS handover** matches upstream's shim exactly.
  - **orca.nix code:** the `''${...}` escaping, the column-0 heredoc after Nix's indent stripping, and `placeholder "out"` inside the quoted heredoc are all correct.

import sys
f=sys.argv[1]; s=open(f).read()
def rep(old,new):
    global s
    assert s.count(old)==1, old[:70]
    s=s.replace(old,new)
rep('''# `orca-ide open` spawns the GUI detached, then exits. Each GUI wrapper layer
# execs the next, so the GUI's bwrap is the CLI's own child; with
# --die-with-parent it would be SIGKILLed the moment `open` returns.
bash -c 'ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$1" -e "
  setTimeout(() => require(\\"fs\\").writeFileSync(process.argv[1], \\"alive\\"), 3000);
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 4000);" "$2" >/dev/null 2>&1 &' _ "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" "$T/alive"''','''# `orca-ide open` spawns the GUI detached, waits for it (up to 15s), then
# exits. Each GUI wrapper layer execs the next, so the GUI's bwrap is the
# CLI's own child; with --die-with-parent it would be SIGKILLed the moment
# `open` returns. The parent here stays up past bwrap's startup, as `open`
# does: one that exits first never arms bwrap's parent-death signal at all.
bash -c 'ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$1" -e "
  setTimeout(() => require(\\"fs\\").writeFileSync(process.argv[1], \\"alive\\"), 4000);
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 5000);" "$2" >/dev/null 2>&1 & sleep 2' _ "$GUI/bin/orca-ide-app" "$T/alive"''')
rep('''# ${!ORCA_@}, not compgen: CI's bash is built without programmable completion.''','''# ${!ORCA_@}, not compgen: it works in a bash built without programmable
# completion too.''')
rep('''# `orca-ide open` spawns ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE, or else process.execPath --
# which under plain node is node itself. Exactly the profile's GUI: the
# unwrapped one has an orca-ide-app too, minus nixGL.''','''# Under plain node, `orca-ide open` has no Orca binary to spawn but
# ORCA_APP_EXECUTABLE (without it, it fails, and `serve` refuses to start).
# Exactly the profile's GUI: the unwrapped one has an orca-ide-app too,
# minus nixGL.''')
rep('''rev=$(nix eval --raw "$HM.home.file" --apply 'f: f.".claude/skills/orca-cli".source' | sed''','''rev=$(nix eval --raw "$HM.home.file" --apply 'f: f.".claude/skills/orca-cli".source' 2>/dev/null | sed''')
open(f,"w").write(s)
PYEOF
sed -i 's|^    dieWithParent = false;|    dieWithParent = true; # TEMP regression check|' orca.nix && git add -A && tests/orca-cli-skills.sh 2>&1 | grep -E 'lifetime|outlives|[0-9]+/[0-9]+ passed'; sed -i 's|^    dieWithParent = true; # TEMP regression check|    dieWithParent = false;|' orca.nix && git add -A && git diff --cached orca.nix | grep -c dieWithParent

Round 2's blocking findings are fixed and committed (`b1d69074`). Round 3 of review is running. `tests/orca-cli-skills.sh` passes 24/24 and `tests/sandbox-fonts.sh` 5/5.

**Fixed in round 2:**
1. **The Wayland flag rule matches Orca's own.** The wrapper used to treat any argument starting with `--ozone-platform` as an explicit choice, including `--ozone-platform-hint`. That would have let Orca fall back to X11 on a host with no X server. Now only `--ozone-platform` or `--ozone-platform=…` before a `--` counts.
2. **The GUI wrapper's flag logic is tested without launching anything.** The test runs the real generated wrapper with its final `exec` swapped for `printf`. Six cases are covered: normal launch, caller's platform wins, `-hint`, `--`, a separate-argument platform, and node mode.
3. **The test can't leave a real GUI behind.** If node mode ever breaks, the GUI-lifetime case is now skipped instead of launching a window. The node-mode check also writes to a file rather than a pipe, so it can't hang on a stray GUI.
4. **One comment was wrong:** it said bare `orca` is safe because the profile comes first on `PATH`. Here `/usr/bin` actually comes first. It's safe only because the screen reader isn't installed.

**Next:** two clean review rounds in a row, then I merge to master and run `hms`, about 10–15 minutes.

Round 3's blocking findings are fixed and committed (`c8b36177`), and review round 4 is running. The test passes 24/24 and the fonts test 5/5.

**What changed:**
1. **The test can't open a stray Orca window.** The two checks that launch the GUI binary now run with no display set. If node mode ever broke, the launch would stop at Orca's display check instead of opening a window.
2. **The Wayland flag rule matches what Orca actually checks.** Only `--ozone-platform=<value>` counts as the caller picking a platform. A bare `--ozone-platform x11` gives Chromium an empty value, so Orca would fall back to X11.
3. **A PATH comment was wrong.** The repo puts `~/.nix-profile/bin` ahead of `/usr/bin` on purpose (`env.nix`). Only this sandboxed Orca shell has it the other way round.
4. **The tests are sturdier:**
   - The flag-logic harness no longer picks up `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` from the calling shell.
   - It refuses a wrapper that has a second launch line.
   - The window-lifetime check gets more slack on a slow start, and still fails if `dieWithParent` is switched back on.

Round 3 was the first round on this branch where correctness came back clean. Security/quality still found two real issues, so I'm still waiting for two clean rounds in a row. After that I merge to master and run `hms`, which takes about 10–15 minutes.

This one read Orca's code more carefully: Chromium keeps the last value of a repeated switch, so prepending changes nothing there, and my comment describes a mechanism that doesn't exist.

The simplest fix is to go back to upstream's own rule, which counts a bare `--ozone-platform` as explicit, and drop the made-up explanation. I'll also unset `WAYLAND_SOCKET` in the test probes and fix two wording nits. Waiting for the correctness reviewer first.

I wrote nothing to the repo and launched no non-node-mode Orca. My only temp file was `alive-r4` in the scratchpad, which I removed.
  
  **What I checked against the build and the app code**
  - I evaluated `.#homeConfigurations.shiori` in the worktree. It gives GUI `/nix/store/REDACTED.4.238` and CLI `/nix/store/bcxlgbildm4ar5harx9p478m2shm0ajp-orca-cli-1.4.238`. The generated inner wrapper (`/nix/store/v0hd7x8b…-orca-1.4.238/bin/orca-ide-app`) contains exactly the `--ozone-platform=?*` loop and one `exec …/.orca-ide-unwrapped "$@"` line at column 0, so the harness's sed and its single-exec guard both match.
  - **Node mode without a display works.** Under `env -u WAYLAND_DISPLAY -u DISPLAY`, `orca-ide-app -p …` printed `node-ok:24.22.0:false:1` and exited 0.
  - **The lifetime case works.** I ran the exact line-122 command. The parent returned after about 4s, the alive marker appeared, and the child exited by itself at 7s, leaving no background process.
  - **A GUI launched by mistake with no display exits; it does not hang or reach the running Orca.**
    - In `out/main/index.js`, the gate `dPn` is checked before `requestSingleInstanceLock` (the `!dPn()` call is at byte 3487054, the `pDn(W.app,e.requestDesktopActivation)` call at 3488484). So a stray launch exits 1 before it can forward argv to a running instance.
    - The gate is skipped only for `--serve` in argv. Neither probe passes it.
    - With no `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, `hPn` is false. With no `DISPLAY`, `_Q` is false. That holds whatever the flag or the hint says.
    - In practice Chromium probably fails even earlier, in platform init: `XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland` is still set, and libwayland falls back to `wayland-0`, but this host's only socket is `wayland-1` (see the nit on line 106 below).
  - **The serve-restart comment is accurate** (orca.nix:59-61). `FEn`/`PEn` skip the X11 re-exec when argv has `--ozone-platform` or `--ozone-platform=…`, and the CLI's serve appends `--ozone-platform=x11` itself (`shared/headless-serve-ozone-platform.js`).
  - **The PATH comment is accurate** (orca.nix:123-124). `env.nix:35` puts `~/.nix-profile/bin` first.
  - **Each argv case goes red on its regression:**
    - `open` catches a missing prepend.
    - `--serve --ozone-platform=x11` catches a prepend that always fires.
    - Bare `--ozone-platform x11` catches a revert to the round-2 rule.
    - `-hint` catches a prefix match.
    - `--` catches a loop with no break.
    - The node-mode case catches dropping the `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` check.
    - `argv()` now unsets the caller's `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`, which closes the false-green hole from round 3.
  - **CI viability is unchanged by this commit.** `env -u`, `timeout`, `seq` and `paste` are all coreutils, which `nix-eval.yml`'s `nix shell` provides. The bwrap/nixGL probes running in the privileged container were already a dependency before c8b36177; I could not check them from here.
  
  **Critical:** none.
  
  **Important:** none.
  
  **Nits**
  1. **The new "falls back to X11" claim is wrong** (tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:77-80; also orca.nix:56-58 and the commit message's "which the gate turns into X11").
     - `dPn` treats an empty `ozone-platform` value as unset. It then uses the hint, or else accepts either endpoint: `_Q(e.DISPLAY)||hPn(e)`. It does not pick X11.
     - Chromium's `base::CommandLine` keeps the last value of a repeated switch. So for `--ozone-platform x11` (and `--ozone-platform=`), the prepended `--ozone-platform=wayland` is overridden by the later empty value, and the prepend does nothing in that case.
     - Behaviour is harmless, but the rationale for the `=?*` change is not what the code does. The comment should say the bare form is malformed and the prepend is moot, not that it is rescued.
  2. **"Picks X11" contradicts `dPn`** (tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:75-76 repeats orca.nix:46-47, which predates this branch). With neither the flag nor the hint, the gate accepts X11 or Wayland. Also, this host has `/tmp/.X11-unix/X0` and `DISPLAY=:0`, so "no X server" is shaky here. I can't reconcile the "measured exit 1" note with this version's code without launching the GUI, which I did not do.
  3. **The line-106 comment overstates the gate's role** (tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:104-106, "it exits at Orca's gate instead"). More precisely, it exits in Chromium platform init, or failing that at Orca's gate, both before any window or single-instance handoff. The conclusion stands.
  4. **No case for `--ozone-platform=` with an empty value** (tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:87-91). A regression from `=?*` to `=*` would go unnoticed. It would also have no runtime effect (see nit 1), so either add the case or drop the `?` distinction from the comments.
  5. **`nodisplay` leaves `WAYLAND_SOCKET` set** (tests/orca-cli-skills.sh:107). `hPn` accepts a numeric `WAYLAND_SOCKET`, so if a caller had it set, a mistaken GUI launch would pass the gate. It is rarely set; adding `-u WAYLAND_SOCKET` closes it.
  6. **The hidden launcher is on PATH** (orca.nix:69-80). Because the nixGL output symlinks `bin/.orca-ide-unwrapped`, it lands on the profile PATH. This is harmless, and `tests/sandbox-fonts.sh:45` relies on it (`-f` follows the symlink), so this is just a note.
</agent-message>

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
orca: an explicit platform is upstream's rule again; drop a made-up reason

Review round 4. Round 3 narrowed the GUI wrapper's "caller named a
platform" test to `--ozone-platform=<value>`, on the claim that Orca's
display gate turns an empty value into X11. It does not: the gate treats
an empty value as unset and accepts either display, and Chromium keeps
the last of a repeated switch, so prepending before a bare or empty
`--ozone-platform` changed nothing. Back to Orca's own
hasExplicitOzonePlatform rule (bare or `=...`, before `--`), with the
bare and empty forms pinned in the argv cases.

The test's no-display probes also unset WAYLAND_SOCKET, which Orca
takes as a live Wayland display. Wording: the CLI's serve appends x11;
two orca-ide bins in the profile collide, not shadow.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git fetch -q origin && git log --oneline HEAD..origin/master | head -3; git log --oneline -1
